title: Samsung, Micron, SK Hynix Lose Bid to Dismiss DRAM Suit
summary: Federal court allows DRAM price-fixing class action to proceed against Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix. What the ruling means for AI chip supply chains.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- A federal court rejected Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix's motions to dismiss a class-action lawsuit alleging DRAM price coordination.
- The ruling allows plaintiffs to proceed with discovery, but does not establish guilt or validate conspiracy claims at this stage.
- The case adds regulatory pressure as AI training demands push DRAM prices higher and supply chain scrutiny intensifies across the semiconductor industry.


A U.S. federal court has denied motions to dismiss a proposed class-action lawsuit accusing Samsung Electronics, Micron Technology, and SK hynix of coordinating DRAM prices. The ruling, officially released on November 16, 2026, allows plaintiffs to proceed with discovery and move the case toward trial, though it stops short of validating any conspiracy claims or establishing liability.


## What the Court Decided


The defendants argued that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege an antitrust conspiracy under the Sherman Act. Judges reviewing the motion found sufficient preliminary evidence to justify further proceedings, including internal communications, pricing patterns, and market-share data submitted by the plaintiff group. The decision does not constitute a finding of wrongdoing but clears the procedural threshold for the case to advance.


Legal experts note that surviving a motion to dismiss is common in complex antitrust litigation. Plaintiffs must still prove coordinated conduct through discovery and expert testimony. Defendants retain the option to seek summary judgment or settlement before trial.


## DRAM Market Context and AI Demand


The three companies collectively control over 90 percent of global DRAM production, a concentration that has drawn regulatory scrutiny across multiple jurisdictions. DRAM prices have risen sharply since early 2025 as generative AI workloads demand high-bandwidth memory for training clusters. Nvidia's HBM3E specifications and hyperscaler purchases have strained supply, compounding price pressures.


Plaintiffs allege that the defendants exploited this tight supply environment by coordinating output reductions and price floors. Samsung, Micron, and SK hynix have consistently denied any collusion, attributing price movements to supply-demand fundamentals and capital expenditure cycles.


## Implications for AI Infrastructure Buyers


Cloud providers, OEMs, and AI labs purchasing DRAM in bulk face uncertainty as the case unfolds. If the lawsuit ultimately succeeds, damages could reach billions of dollars and trigger supply-chain audits. More immediately, the discovery phase may reveal internal pricing strategies and capacity-planning documents that influence future procurement negotiations.


Industry analysts expect the case to run for at least two years before reaching a verdict or settlement. Meanwhile, antitrust regulators in the European Union and South Korea have opened parallel investigations into memory-chip pricing practices.


## Availability


The court's ruling was officially released on November 16, 2026, following months of sealed briefings and oral arguments. Public access to discovery materials will depend on protective orders negotiated between counsel and approved by the presiding judge.


## What This Means


This procedural milestone shifts the DRAM antitrust case from pleading stage to evidence-gathering. While a failed dismissal bid is not proof of conspiracy, it signals that courts view the plaintiffs' allegations as serious enough to warrant full investigation. For AI infrastructure buyers and memory-chip consumers, the case underscores ongoing supply-chain risks and the potential for regulatory intervention in concentrated semiconductor markets. Expect heightened attention to pricing transparency and capacity announcements from all three defendants as discovery proceeds through 2027.
